title: Community Ecology and Biodiversity
subject: AP Biology
objectives: Describe species interactions: competition, predation, and the forms of symbiosis
Explain the competitive exclusion principle, ecological niches, and resource partitioning
Describe keystone species, ecological succession, and how communities change over time
Explain why biodiversity matters for ecosystem stability and resilience

sections.heading: The Web of Who Affects Whom
sections.content:
A population never lives alone. In any real habitat, dozens or hundreds of species share space — eating each other, competing, helping, and harming — and the tangle of these interactions is what we call a community: all the different populations of different species living and interacting in the same area. If population ecology (last lesson) asked how ONE species' numbers change, community ecology asks how species AFFECT EACH OTHER, and how those interactions shape who lives where and in what abundance.

The interactions fall into a few classic categories, and a simple bookkeeping trick organizes them: for each pair of species in an interaction, ask whether each one is helped (+), harmed (−), or unaffected (0). Competition is (−/−): both are harmed by fighting over the same limited resource. Predation (and herbivory and parasitism) is (+/−): one benefits, the other is harmed. The symbioses — long-term close relationships — split by their sign pattern: mutualism (+/+, both benefit), commensalism (+/0, one benefits, the other unaffected), and parasitism (+/−, one benefits, the host is harmed). This +/−/0 framework lets you classify any interaction the exam throws at you.

These interactions aren't just a catalog — they are the forces that, together with the limiting factors from the last lesson, determine community structure: which species coexist, how abundant each is, and how the whole assemblage responds to change. We'll move from pairwise interactions to the niche concept, then to how communities shift over time and why their diversity matters.

sections.heading: Competition, Niches, and Resource Partitioning
sections.content:
When two species need the SAME limited resource, they compete, and competition (−/−) harms both. This leads to one of ecology's foundational ideas: the competitive exclusion principle, which states that two species competing for the EXACT same limiting resource cannot coexist indefinitely in the same place — one will be slightly better at exploiting the resource and will eventually drive the other to local extinction. Two species can't occupy the identical ecological niche.

What's a niche? An ecological niche is the full role a species plays in its community — all the resources it uses and conditions it needs: what it eats, where and when it's active, the temperature and habitat it requires, and so on. It's often summarized as a species' 'occupation' or 'way of life,' as opposed to its habitat (its 'address'). The fundamental niche is the full range of conditions a species COULD use; the realized niche is the (usually smaller) range it ACTUALLY uses once competitors and other limits are accounted for.

So how do similar species coexist if competitive exclusion is so strict? Through resource partitioning: competing species divide up resources or niche space so they're not using the EXACT same thing, reducing direct competition. The classic example is Robert MacArthur's warblers — several warbler species feed in the same spruce trees but in DIFFERENT zones (one in the treetop, one in the mid-branches, one near the trunk), partitioning the tree so each has its own slice. Resource partitioning is also a driver of evolution: competition can select for slight differences (character displacement) that let species specialize and coexist — connecting community ecology straight back to natural selection (Unit 7).

sections.question: Two species of barnacle live on the same rocks; when one is experimentally removed, the other expands into the zone it previously couldn't occupy. This expansion from realized to fundamental niche is most directly explained by...
options: the removal of interspecific competition that had restricted the species' niche
the competitive exclusion principle being false
sections.explanation: The expanded barnacle had been restricted to a smaller realized niche by competition with the other species. Removing the competitor eliminated that pressure, letting it occupy more of its fundamental niche. This is the classic Connell barnacle experiment, illustrating that competition (−/−) shapes the realized niche — not mutualism or predation.

sections.heading: Species Interactions (+/−/0 Framework)
rows: Both harmed by sharing a limited resource
Lion and zebra; bird and insect
Parasite benefits, host is harmed (often lives on/in host)
Tapeworm in an intestine; tick on a dog
Bee and flower; gut bacteria and human
One benefits, the other is unaffected
Barnacles on a whale; birds nesting in a tree

sections.heading: Predation, Defenses, and Keystone Species
sections.content:
Predation (+/−) is more than lions eating zebras — it's a powerful evolutionary force that drives an 'arms race' (coevolution, Unit 7) between predators and prey. Prey have evolved spectacular DEFENSES: camouflage (blending in), mechanical defenses (spines, shells), and chemical defenses (toxins). Two warning-related patterns are favorites on the exam. Aposematic (warning) coloration is bright coloring that advertises that a prey species is toxic or dangerous (a poison dart frog's vivid hues) — predators learn to avoid it. Mimicry exploits this: in Batesian mimicry, a HARMLESS species evolves to LOOK like a harmful one (a harmless fly mimicking a wasp's stripes), gaining protection it doesn't 'deserve'; in Müllerian mimicry, two or more genuinely HARMFUL species evolve to resemble each OTHER, so predators learn one warning pattern and avoid them all.

Not all species matter equally to a community. A keystone species has an effect on its community far larger than its abundance would suggest — like the keystone at the top of a stone arch, remove it and the whole structure collapses. The classic case is the sea star Pisaster: when ecologist Robert Paine removed sea stars from tidal zones, the mussels they preyed on exploded in number and crowded out other species, and biodiversity crashed. The sea star, though not abundant, held the whole community's diversity together by keeping a dominant competitor in check. Sea otters are another keystone: by eating sea urchins, they protect kelp forests (urchins devour kelp), so otters indirectly sustain an entire ecosystem. Keystone species are a major focus of conservation precisely because losing them triggers disproportionate, cascading change.

sections.heading: Classifying Interactions and Tracing a Keystone Effect
sections.content:
Two AP skills: classifying a symbiosis with the +/−/0 framework, and predicting the ripple effects of removing a keystone species.

Part 1 — Classify these relationships. (a) Clownfish live among a sea anemone's stinging tentacles: the clownfish gains protection from predators, and the anemone gets cleaned and defended by the clownfish. Both benefit → MUTUALISM (+/+). (b) A remora fish attaches to a shark and eats scraps from the shark's kills; the shark is neither helped nor harmed. One benefits, one unaffected → COMMENSALISM (+/0). (c) A tick feeds on a deer's blood, harming the deer. One benefits, host harmed → PARASITISM (+/−). The method: identify each partner's outcome (+, −, or 0), then match the sign pattern to the interaction name.

Part 2 — Trace a keystone removal. Sea otters (keystone) eat sea urchins; sea urchins eat kelp. Predict what happens if otters are hunted out. Step 1: with otters gone, urchins are no longer controlled, so the urchin population BOOMS (a density effect, last lesson). Step 2: exploding urchins overgraze the kelp forest, destroying it ('urchin barrens'). Step 3: the kelp forest was habitat and food for countless fish and invertebrates, so its loss collapses biodiversity across the community — a trophic CASCADE. The exam reward: don't stop at 'urchins increase'; trace the chain through at least two more links to the community-wide consequence, and name it a keystone/cascade effect. This shows you understand that one species can control an entire community's structure.

sections.heading: Succession and Why Biodiversity Matters
sections.content:
Communities aren't static — they change over time through ecological succession, the predictable sequence of communities that replace one another in an area. Primary succession begins on bare substrate with NO soil — newly cooled lava, a retreating glacier's bare rock. The first colonizers are hardy pioneer species like lichens and mosses, which break down rock and, as they die, build the first thin soil. That soil lets small plants, then larger plants and shrubs, then trees move in, each stage modifying the environment and enabling the next, until a relatively stable mature community develops. Secondary succession occurs where a disturbance (a fire, a flood, an abandoned farm field) destroyed a community but the SOIL remains — so it proceeds much FASTER, because soil, seeds, and roots are already present. The key contrast: primary starts from bare rock (no soil); secondary starts with soil intact.

All of this leads to biodiversity — the variety of life, measured as the number of different species (species richness) and their relative abundance (evenness) in a community. Biodiversity is not just an aesthetic value; it makes ecosystems more STABLE and RESILIENT — better able to withstand and recover from disturbances like disease, drought, or invasion. The logic is a bit like a diversified investment portfolio: a community with many species has built-in backups. If a disturbance wipes out one species, others can fill its role, so ecosystem functions (energy capture, nutrient cycling, pollination) keep running. A low-diversity ecosystem, like a single-crop farm field (a monoculture), is fragile — one pest or disease can devastate the whole thing. Greater genetic diversity within species (Unit 7) similarly buffers populations against change. This is the scientific core of why biodiversity loss — the theme of the final lesson — is so dangerous: every species lost removes a thread from the web, and a frayed web holds together less well.

steps.title: Classify the species interactions
steps.content: For each pair of interacting species, assign + (helped), − (harmed), or 0 (unaffected) to each. Match the sign pattern: competition (−/−), predation/parasitism/herbivory (+/−), mutualism (+/+), commensalism (+/0).

steps.title: Identify niches and competition outcomes
steps.content: Determine each species' niche (its role and resource use). Recall that two species can't occupy the identical niche indefinitely (competitive exclusion); coexistence usually requires resource partitioning.

steps.title: Look for keystone species and cascades
steps.content: Identify any species whose influence far exceeds its abundance. Predict the cascading, community-wide effects of adding or removing it by tracing the chain through multiple trophic links.

steps.title: Consider change over time and diversity
steps.content: Determine whether the community is undergoing succession (primary from bare rock, secondary from intact soil) and assess its biodiversity, which increases stability and resilience to disturbance.

sections.question: Why does an ecosystem with high biodiversity tend to be more stable and resilient than a low-diversity one like a single-crop farm field?
options: More species always means less competition
With many species, others can compensate or fill a role if one is lost, so ecosystem functions continue despite disturbances
Biodiversity prevents any species from ever going extinct
sections.explanation: High biodiversity provides functional 'backups': if a disturbance removes one species, others can fill its role, so processes like nutrient cycling and energy capture keep running — the ecosystem resists and recovers from disturbance. A monoculture lacks these backups, so a single pest or disease can devastate it. Diversity doesn't eliminate competition or disturbances or guarantee no extinctions; it buffers the system's functions against change.

sections.content: Communities are shaped by species interactions classified with the +/−/0 framework: competition (−/−), predation/parasitism/herbivory (+/−), mutualism (+/+), and commensalism (+/0). The competitive exclusion principle means species can't share the identical niche, so coexistence requires resource partitioning; keystone species exert outsized control (removing them triggers cascades); communities change through primary succession (from bare rock) or secondary succession (from intact soil); and biodiversity increases ecosystem stability and resilience.

sections.heading: Community Ecology Traps to Avoid
sections.content: (1) Use the +/−/0 signs carefully: mutualism (+/+), commensalism (+/0), parasitism (+/−), competition (−/−). Commensalism's second species is UNAFFECTED (0), not harmed. (2) The competitive exclusion principle says two species can't occupy the IDENTICAL niche indefinitely — similar species coexist by resource PARTITIONING. (3) Niche = a species' role/'occupation'; habitat = its 'address.' Don't equate them. (4) Batesian mimicry = a HARMLESS species mimics a harmful one; Müllerian = two HARMFUL species resemble each other. (5) A KEYSTONE species has large impact despite LOW abundance — it's not the most common species. (6) Primary succession starts on bare rock with NO soil (slow); secondary starts with soil intact (faster). Don't swap them.

sections.heading: Cascades, Wolves, and the Hidden Architecture of Nature
sections.content:
The most dramatic lesson of community ecology is how tightly the fates of species are woven together — and how a single change can ripple across an entire landscape. The reintroduction of gray wolves to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 is the textbook demonstration. Wolves had been exterminated decades earlier, and without them elk populations had exploded and overgrazed the valleys, stripping young willows and aspens along the rivers. When wolves returned, they preyed on elk and, just as importantly, changed elk BEHAVIOR (the behavioral ecology of this unit's first lesson) — elk avoided open river valleys where they were vulnerable. Relieved of grazing pressure, willows and aspens regrew; beavers returned to use the willows and built dams; the dams created wetlands for fish, amphibians, and birds; songbird and pollinator diversity rose; and stabilized banks even changed how the rivers flowed. One predator, a keystone species, cascaded through the whole community and reshaped a physical landscape. Whether every link is as strong as the popular story claims is still debated by ecologists, but the core point stands: top predators can structure entire ecosystems, and removing them (as humans so often do) unravels far more than the predator itself.

This interconnectedness is exactly why biodiversity is not a luxury but the load-bearing architecture of functioning ecosystems — and why its loss is the great ecological crisis of our time, the subject of the final lesson. Every species occupies a niche and participates in interactions; each one is a thread, and the redundancy of many threads is what lets the web absorb shocks. Coral reefs and tropical rainforests, the most biodiverse ecosystems on Earth, provide outsized services to humanity — fisheries, storm protection, medicines, climate regulation — precisely because of their dense interaction networks. When biodiversity erodes through habitat destruction, overharvesting, invasive species, pollution, and climate change, ecosystems lose resilience and can flip abruptly to degraded states (a reef bleaching into rubble, a forest becoming grassland) that are hard to reverse. The mutualisms matter too: roughly a third of human food crops depend on animal pollinators, so the decline of bees is not a sentimental concern but a community-ecology problem with direct stakes for food security.

Community ecology completes the bottom-up logic of this unit. Individual behavior (lesson 1) governs how organisms interact; energy flow (lesson 2) sets the trophic structure those interactions occur within; population dynamics (lesson 3) determine each species' abundance and its density-dependent pressures — which ARE the competition, predation, and disease of community ecology; and now these interactions, scaled across many species, build the communities and ecosystems whose biodiversity determines stability. Natural selection (Unit 7) is the thread running through all of it: predator-prey arms races, mutualistic coadaptation, resource partitioning, and mimicry are all evolution operating within the ecological web. Understanding how communities are assembled and held together — and how easily they can be pulled apart — is the essential foundation for confronting the human-driven disruptions that close the course.

sections.heading: How AP Tests Community Ecology
sections.content: Point-winners: (1) Classify interactions with the +/−/0 framework (mutualism +/+, commensalism +/0, parasitism/predation +/−, competition −/−). (2) Apply the competitive exclusion principle and explain coexistence via resource partitioning; distinguish niche from habitat and fundamental from realized niche. (3) Identify a keystone species and TRACE a removal/addition through multiple trophic links to the community-wide cascade. (4) Distinguish Batesian (harmless mimics harmful) from Müllerian (harmful resemble each other) mimicry and explain aposematic coloration. (5) Contrast primary (bare rock, no soil) vs. secondary (soil intact) succession. (6) Explain WHY biodiversity increases stability/resilience (functional backups). Command words: 'predict' a cascade and 'explain' the mechanism, not just the first step.

aiContext: This AP Biology Unit 8 lesson covers community ecology and biodiversity (CED topics 8.4, 8.7, and ecosystem-level interactions). A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in one area; community ecology studies how species affect each other. THE organizing tool: the +/−/0 framework — assign each partner helped (+), harmed (−), or unaffected (0): competition (−/−, both harmed by sharing a limited resource), predation/herbivory/parasitism (+/−, one benefits/one harmed), mutualism (+/+, both benefit — bee/flower, gut bacteria), commensalism (+/0, one benefits/other unaffected — barnacles on a whale). Common error: treating commensalism's second species as harmed (it's unaffected). Competition leads to the COMPETITIVE EXCLUSION PRINCIPLE: two species can't occupy the IDENTICAL niche (use the exact same limiting resource) indefinitely — one outcompetes the other. NICHE = a species' full role/'occupation' (resources used, conditions needed), vs. HABITAT = its 'address'; fundamental niche (could use) vs. realized niche (actually uses after competition — Connell's barnacle experiment). Similar species coexist via RESOURCE PARTITIONING (MacArthur's warblers feeding in different tree zones), which can drive character displacement (links to natural selection, Unit 7). Predation drives coevolutionary arms races and prey DEFENSES: camouflage, mechanical (spines/shells), chemical (toxins), aposematic/warning coloration (advertises toxicity — poison dart frog), and MIMICRY — Batesian (a HARMLESS species mimics a harmful one) vs. Müllerian (two or more HARMFUL species resemble each other). KEYSTONE species have impact far exceeding their abundance (Paine's sea star Pisaster; sea otters protecting kelp by eating urchins); removing them triggers trophic CASCADES — students must trace the chain through multiple links, not stop at the first effect. Communities change via ECOLOGICAL SUCCESSION: primary (starts on bare substrate with NO soil — lava, glacier retreat; pioneer species like lichens/mosses build soil; slow) vs. secondary (disturbance left SOIL intact — fire, abandoned field; faster). BIODIVERSITY (species richness + evenness) increases ecosystem STABILITY and RESILIENCE via functional redundancy/backups — high-diversity systems resist and recover from disturbance, while monocultures are fragile; analogous to a diversified portfolio, and parallels genetic diversity within species (Unit 7). Key misconceptions to counter: mis-signing interactions (esp. commensalism), thinking similar species share identical niches, equating niche with habitat, swapping Batesian/Müllerian mimicry, thinking a keystone species is the most abundant, and swapping primary/secondary succession. Examples: Yellowstone wolf reintroduction (keystone cascade + behavioral change), pollinator mutualisms and food security. Connects to behavior (lesson 1), energy flow/trophic structure (lesson 2), population density-dependent factors = competition/predation/disease (lesson 3), natural selection (Unit 7 arms races/coadaptation), and forward to biodiversity loss (final lesson). On the exam expect interaction classification, competitive exclusion/resource partitioning, keystone cascade tracing, mimicry/succession distinctions, and biodiversity-stability reasoning.
